sources.title: The King: birth, education, Prince of Wales title and investiture, and accession
sources.findings: Read the Royal Household biography’s accession, early-life, education and investiture sections. It confirms birth at Buckingham Palace on 14 November 1948, Trinity College entry in 1967, archaeology/anthropology followed by history, and a degree in 1970. Prince of Wales title was conferred in 1958, whereas investiture took place on 1 July 1969; these are not interchangeable dates. He became King on Elizabeth II’s death on 8 September 2022, not at the 2023 coronation. The biography’s historical Prince of Wales wording is not treated as his current title.

sources.publisher: UCL Constitution Unit / Lisa James and Robert Hazell
sources.title: April 2024: constitutional monarchy, conventions and competing democratic arguments
sources.findings: Read UCL Constitution Unit’s April 2024 briefing by Lisa James and Robert Hazell. It distinguishes formal constitutional powers from convention and ministerial advice, and describes government policy as the responsibility of elected political institutions. Preserve both supporters’ symbolic-unity argument and republicans’ objection to an unelected head of state. No claim that the monarch has no formal legal powers, independently controls ordinary policy or personally authored the government’s King’s Speech. Historical polling figures are not reused as current 2026 public opinion.

sources.title: Commonwealth organisation and non-hereditary symbolic headship
sources.findings: Read Commonwealth Secretariat organisational page, especially headship and secretariat sections. Charles III is the symbolic Head of the Commonwealth; the role is not hereditary and future holders are chosen by member-country leaders. The Secretary-General manages the Secretariat. Parts of this page still describe the November 2026 summit as future and list the preceding Chair-in-Office, so those stale fields are not carried into current biography. Do not equate headship with sovereign rule over every member.

sources.title: 17 November 2026: text of the address at the inauguration of the 12th General Synod
sources.findings: Read the Royal Household’s 17 November 2026 text for the inauguration of the 12th General Synod of the Church of England. It addresses faith, cohesion and relationships across faith communities. The timeline explicitly records publication of the official speech text; no video inspection or independent verification of exact delivery time is claimed. Church of England is not all Anglican churches worldwide, and religious views are attributed to the speaker rather than endorsed as factual propositions.

sources.title: Court Circular: 16 November 2026 visits to Preston and the National Cyber Force headquarters
sources.findings: Read the 16 November 2026 Buckingham Palace entry in the Court Circular. It records actual visits to the Harris in Preston, the Flag Market and the National Cyber Force headquarters, including received briefings. This is a completed-engagement record, not the future Royal Diary. Other entries for the Princess Royal and the Prince of Wales are not attributed to Charles. The birthday notice alone is not the life-status evidence; no operational cyber capabilities or health outcome are inferred.

sources.title: 3 November 2026: CHOGM opening speech in St John’s, Antigua
sources.findings: Read the opening and relevant substantive paragraphs of the 3 November 2026 CHOGM speech in St John’s, Antigua. Charles speaks as King and Head of the Commonwealth, expresses personal sorrow over the transatlantic slave trade and advocates youth opportunity and climate resilience. Sorrow is not a formal government reparations commitment or proof that historic disputes have been resolved. The date is a completed speech record, distinct from the August tour announcement. No claim that his statements constitute consensus policy of every Commonwealth state.

sources.publisher: University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
sources.title: 30 April 2024: King and Queen visit patients and staff at the Macmillan Cancer Centre
sources.findings: Read UCLH’s 30 April 2024 host-institution report. It confirms Charles and Camilla’s actual visit to the University College Hospital Macmillan Cancer Centre, meetings with patients and staff, and his new Cancer Research UK patronage. Participants’ cancer types and treatments are not assigned to the King. Descriptions of experimental or innovative treatments do not demonstrate their effectiveness or identify his treatment regime.

sources.title: 30 April 2024: return to public-facing duties while treatment continued
sources.findings: Read ITV News’s 30 April 2024 account of the resumption of public-facing duties after the February cancer announcement. Its quoted palace statement explicitly says treatment continued. Preserve historical timing and avoid interpreting return to duties as cure, or its broad first-public-appearance wording as an absence of every earlier public or official activity. No cancer type, stage, prognosis or current treatment schedule is inferred.

sources.publisher: House of Commons Library / David Torrance
sources.title: 28 April 2025 briefing: the 6 May 2023 coronation and its constitutional context
sources.findings: Read the Commons Library’s 28 April 2025 webpage summary of the coronation research briefing. It confirms that Charles and Camilla’s coronation took place on 6 May 2023 at Westminster Abbey and explains the ceremony’s relationship to accession. This is not a claim to have read the full linked PDF. The report publication date, advance October 2022 announcement, May 2023 ceremony and September 2022 succession remain separate.

sources.title: 22 January 2020: launch of the Sustainable Markets Initiative with the Prince of Wales
sources.findings: Read the World Economic Forum’s contemporary 22 January 2020 launch release. It identifies the Sustainable Markets Initiative as a collaboration with the then Prince of Wales, announced at Davos. Ten-point transition proposals and planned roundtables are goals or plans, not measured global emission cuts. Preserve collective organisational roles; do not credit Charles with unilateral market regulation or claim that the later incorporated company already existed in its current legal form in 2020.

sources.title: History: 1976 youth pilot projects, 2023 renaming announcement and 2024 formal name change
sources.findings: Read the King’s Trust Group history. The 1976 entry describes youth pilots funded by naval severance pay; later entries distinguish the 1999 royal-charter consolidation, 2015 international launch and 2018 group network. The initial UK projects are not conflated with every later overseas entity’s foundation date. Renaming intention was announced in 2023 and the formal King’s Trust name came in 2024. Charity-reported beneficiary totals and future impact targets are not independently verified or reproduced.

sources.title: 1970 Cardiff Countryside conference speech, posted to the current site on 13 November 2017
sources.findings: Read the Cardiff Countryside in 1970 speech archive, including its opening and discussion of pollution, waste and urban/rural environments. The page visibly says Published 13/11/2017, but the title and text place the speech in 1970. Retain year precision and do not invent an exact day or claim it was his first environmental speech on the evidence inspected. Historical scientific estimates and examples are not treated as current measurements.

sources.title: Current organisation: founder Charles III and private-sector transition objectives
sources.findings: Read the Sustainable Markets Initiative current homepage, identifying Charles as founder and outlining private-sector transition and finance objectives. Founder is not assumed to mean executive management or personal authorship of all subsequent projects. Proposed mobilisation of finance and latest organisational event announcements are not completed personal investments or evidence of his attendance at those events.

sources.publisher: House of Commons Library / Philip Loft
sources.title: 30 October 2026: Commonwealth governance, realms and UK government priorities
sources.findings: Read the 30 October 2026 Commons Library Commonwealth briefing webpage. It distinguishes symbolic, non-hereditary headship, the realms sharing Charles as monarch, the Secretary-General and rotating Chair-in-Office. Its then-future Antigua summit wording is updated by the 3 November speech evidence. The UK government’s position on reparations is separate from the King’s personal expressions of sorrow. Plans by countries to become republics are not recorded as completed constitutional changes; no current membership count is frozen in the dossier.

portraitReview.unresolved: Read Commons candidate and parent-file descriptions and US presidential-office official-work public-domain declarations. Source is a 10 July 2023 White House/POTUS photograph with Joe Biden. Candidate was cropped that day by TDKR Chicago 101 and its levels adjusted by WikiPedant on 19 September 2023; later upload/edit date is not capture date. Candidate 727×1025; parent file 4096×2731. Preserve source, crop and adjustment credits; do not invent a named photographer or apply this US declaration to every royal image. Original social-media source returned 403 in web open. Candidate download on 18 November 2026 failed with curl 22, proxy HTTP 403 and reported HTTP 000; old referenced cache is absent. Full bytes, identity, colour and crop suitability remain uninspected.
